subject: radiology
title: Radionuclides and Nuclear Medicine Instrumentation

steps.tx: Isotopes share the same **atomic number** but differ in mass number. Isobars share mass number, isotones share neutron number, and isomers share both numbers but sit in different **energy states** within the nucleus. Recognising these four terms is a common NEET-PG starting point.

steps.tx: Radioactive emissions are alpha, beta, gamma and neutrons. Alpha particles are the **least penetrating** but most ionising when internalised. Beta particles are electrons stopped by a few millimetres of tissue. Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with the highest penetration, which is why they are used for imaging.

steps.tx: Physical half-life is the time for radioactivity to fall by half. Tc-99m has a **physical half-life of 6 hours**, Fluorine-18 about 110 minutes, and Iodine-131 about 8 days. Biological half-life is the time the body takes to clear half of a substance, and the **effective half-life** combines both, always shorter than either alone.

steps.tx: The **molybdenum-technetium generator** holds parent Molybdenum-99, which decays to give Technetium-99m. Tc-99m emits pure gamma radiation at a useful energy and has a short half-life, so it is the most widely used diagnostic radiopharmaceutical. Its uses include bone, liver, kidney and cardiac studies, and MIBI for myocardial perfusion.

steps.tx: A gamma camera detects gamma rays using a **sodium iodide scintillating crystal** coupled to photomultiplier tubes, and lead collimators define the direction of origin. Planar imaging and SPECT use gamma cameras, whereas PET uses paired 511 keV annihilation photons from positron emitters such as Fluorine-18 labelled FDG, produced in a cyclotron.
